summary: Kole Jain redesigns a file management app to show the common color mistakes that make beginner UIs look cheap or confusing, arguing that less color is almost always better. He covers cutting competing accent colors, keeping backgrounds neutral (which he calls neutral balance), stretching a small brand palette with analogous and complementary hues, and using grays instead of pure black and white to build hierarchy. He shows that dark mode should be designed on purpose rather than made by inverting light mode, that destructive actions need red even when it is off-brand, and that hover, press and disabled states can be made from lighter, darker and desaturated versions of the base color. For a design system, this gives concrete rules for accent use, neutral surfaces, text grays, dark-mode adjustments, semantic colors and state colors, plus brand examples (Lemon Squeezy, Headspace, Dribbble, Mailchimp, Airbnb).
key_ideas: Less is almost always more with color: not everything should be a different color.
Several accent colors on one screen compete for attention; reducing the palette creates clarity.
The 60-30-10 rule splits a screen into 60% dominant neutral, 30% secondary and 10% accent color.
A brand color on an unimportant element can dominate the page; lighten it and switch its text to black.
Icons are recognizable symbols and mostly need no color; color on icons should signal status, such as an active tab.
Neutral balance works like white space: backgrounds should stay in the background, so start with a neutral gray background and a white or very light foreground.
A neutral gray can carry a hint of the brand hue to add color without overpowering the visuals.
Sometimes the cleanest way to separate a card is a simple border rather than another background layer.
A limited brand palette can be extended by rotating the brand hue slightly (analogous) or crossing the color wheel (complementary).
Brand colors can be adapted, for example darkened, to pass contrast checks and serve good design.
Pure black and white are not wrong, but grays are often the better option for hierarchy; less important text, labels and borders can be gray.
Dark mode is not the inverse of light mode: borders and surfaces need more separation, text should be light gray, and pure white is kept for the most important items.
Destructive actions use red even when the brand color is different, which is why red and green sit in many brand palettes.
Hover is slightly lighter or brighter, press is slightly darker and disabled is desaturated; mobile has no hover, so it relies on press effects.

The seven mistakes the title promises are, in order: too many colors, no neutral balance, being stuck with brand colors, overusing pure black and white, inverting for dark mode, on-brand destructive actions, and missing element states [inferred]

topics.name: Color
topics.summary: Reduce competing accents, follow 60-30-10 loosely, keep backgrounds neutral, extend a small brand palette with analogous and complementary hues, and use grays instead of pure black and white for hierarchy.

topics.name: Dark mode and themes
topics.summary: Do not invert light mode: brighten borders and cards, use light grays for text, reserve pure white for the most important text or actions, lower gray brightness more aggressively, and desaturate the logo a touch.

topics.name: Accessibility
topics.summary: Colored cards and brand colors with white text often fail WCAG contrast checks; lighten backgrounds with black text, darken the brand color, or pick a complementary color that passes.

topics.name: Visual hierarchy
topics.summary: Neutral balance works like white space; secondary information such as file size, type and labels can be dark or light gray instead of black.

topics.name: Buttons and actions
topics.summary: Delete buttons use red rather than the brand color; hover is lighter or brighter, press darker, disabled desaturated, and a light gray button with white text reads as disabled on its own.

topics.name: Icons and imagery

topics.name: Depth, shadows and borders

topics.name: Cards and sections

rules.rule: Do not give each card or element its own accent color; keep one accent and reduce the palette.
rules.why: At least five different accent colors on the cards all compete for attention; reducing the palette creates clarity.
rules.evidence: at least five different accent colors on these cards

rules.rule: Check colored card and text pairs against WCAG contrast and drop colors that fail.
rules.why: Cards that fail the WCAG contrast checks cannot reasonably be used.
rules.evidence: they almost all fail the WCAG contrast checks

rules.rule: Use the 60-30-10 split as a rough check: about 60% dominant neutral, 30% secondary color, 10% accent.
rules.why: Five accents competing for attention is the problem it addresses; the redesign only 'somewhat' hits it, so it works as a guide rather than a strict rule [inferred]
rules.evidence: 603010 rule

rules.rule: When a brand-colored surface belongs to an unimportant element, lighten the color and switch its text to black.
rules.why: The bright brand color dominates the page for an element that isn't important and causes accessibility issues.
rules.evidence: A good fix is to lighten it up

rules.rule: Leave icons uncolored and reserve icon color for status, such as marking the active tab.
rules.why: An icon's job is to be a recognizable symbol; color should communicate status.
rules.evidence: icons need no color

rules.rule: Remove colors that are used only for the sake of using color.
rules.why: Reducing the palette creates more clarity for the user.
rules.evidence: used just for the sake of using color

rules.rule: Do not use bright colors or bright gradients for page backgrounds; start with a neutral gray background and a very light or white foreground.
rules.why: Backgrounds should stay in the background (neutral balance, the color version of white space); the sandy yellow gradient did not.
rules.evidence: Almost never will you want bright colors for your background

rules.rule: In dark mode, put the darker colors in the background and slightly lighter colors in the foreground.
rules.why: Same neutral-balance idea as light mode.
rules.evidence: This is the same idea for a dark mode

rules.rule: Add a hint of the brand hue to neutral grays, or use a light tint of the brand color on card backgrounds, to bring in color without overpowering the visuals.
rules.why: It adds a splash of color without overpowering the visuals (Headspace does this with a tint of its orange on cards).
rules.evidence: adding a hint of purple to it

rules.rule: In light mode, consider reversing the usual background and foreground for smaller UI features such as a search bar.
rules.why: It can give better accessibility for smaller UI features, as in Dribbble's search bar.
rules.evidence: reversing the background and foreground

rules.rule: To separate cards, prefer a simple border over adding another colored background layer.
rules.why: Adding another layer of color to the UI is a lot of clutter; maintaining neutral balance sometimes means removing backgrounds altogether.
rules.evidence: sometimes a simple border is the best solution

rules.rule: When the brand palette is too small, extend it by rotating the brand hue slightly on the color wheel (analogous) or picking the color across the wheel (complementary), rather than only changing opacity.
rules.why: Changing opacity feels bland; analogous and complementary colors work well together on the UI.
rules.evidence: rotate our purple slightly on the color wheel

rules.rule: If a brand color fails WCAG with white text, darken it until it passes or use a complementary color that passes.
rules.why: The orange brand color failed with white text; the darker version and a complementary blue both pass.
rules.evidence: fails WCAG checks with white text

rules.rule: Adapt brand colors when needed to accommodate good design instead of treating brand guidelines as fixed.
rules.why: Many brands do this, such as Mailchimp's yellow with turquoise and Airbnb's bright pink with a deeper pink.
rules.evidence: don't be afraid to adapt brand colors

rules.rule: Use dark gray, not pure black, for less important information such as file size and file type, and the same for labels and borders; well-grouped elements can go lighter still.
rules.why: Hierarchy: this information isn't super important, and because the elements are well grouped they can be lightened.
rules.evidence: we can use a dark gray instead

rules.rule: In light mode, consider a very dark brand hue (such as dark purple) for text instead of pure black.
rules.why: Often there are better options than black or white; most of the redesign's text is light gray or dark purple, not black.
rules.evidence: most of the text is light gray or dark purple, not even black

rules.rule: In dark mode, lower the brightness of grays more aggressively than in light mode and reserve white for only the most important actions.
rules.why: Dark modes have a distinct focus on eye strain.
rules.evidence: Reserving white only for the most important actions

rules.rule: Do not make dark mode by inverting the light-mode colors; build the palette with the goals of dark mode in mind.
rules.why: Inverting gives a result that is not awful but certainly not ideal.
rules.evidence: dark mode is not just the inverse of light mode

rules.rule: In dark mode, brighten borders and main card surfaces more than an inversion would.
rules.why: Dark colors need to be more different than light colors to see the difference.
rules.evidence: brighten up these borders and the main card

rules.rule: In dark mode, use light grays for text and brighten only the most important text (for example the logo and storage used) to pure white.
rules.why: Light grays are easier on the eyes than white.
rules.evidence: light grays work best on dark mode

rules.rule: In dark mode, desaturate the logo a touch.
rules.why: The source gives no reason; its redesign does this when converting to dark mode, while saying the other colors are probably fine.
rules.evidence: our logo should be desaturated a touch

rules.rule: Use red, not the brand color, for destructive actions such as delete.
rules.why: A brand-colored delete button draws attention and doesn't illustrate its destructive nature; it wouldn't fly from a usability point of view.
rules.evidence: Instead, we use red; wouldn't fly from a usability point of view

rules.rule: Include red and green in the palette even when they are not brand colors.
rules.why: Usability needs them, for example for destructive actions.
rules.evidence: red and green are often in a brand's color palette

rules.rule: Notification indicators may use red or the brand color.
rules.why: Notifications are much more flexible than destructive actions.
rules.evidence: Red is also often used for notifications

rules.rule: Make hover states a slightly lighter or brighter version of the base color.
rules.why: Hover and press are the most common element states, and color alone can show them.
rules.evidence: For hover states, use a slightly lighter or brighter version

rules.rule: Make active or pressed states a slightly darker version of the base color.
rules.why: Hover and press are the most common element states, and color alone can show them.
rules.evidence: For an active or press state, use a slightly darker version

rules.rule: Make disabled states by desaturating the color, unless it is already grayscale; a light gray fill with white text reads as disabled on its own.
rules.why: The button is obviously disabled without other visual cues, and this is bulletproof for dark mode too.
rules.evidence: for a disabled state, just desaturate the color

rules.rule: On mobile, where there is no hover, give tappable elements a press state, such as a slightly darker gray on press.
rules.why: It makes it feel like you're actually pressing into something.
rules.evidence: we don't have hover effects on mobile

decisions.question: How should cards that are not the main focus be colored?

options.name: A different bright accent color per card
options.effect: Cards burn the eye, compete for attention and mostly fail WCAG contrast.
options.when: Not recommended.

options.name: Solid brand color
options.effect: Roughly hits 60-30-10, but the bright brand color dominates the page for an unimportant element and causes accessibility issues.
options.when: Not recommended for low-importance elements.

options.name: Lightened brand tint with black text
options.effect: Draws less attention and keeps text readable.
options.when: When the element should carry some brand color.

options.name: No background, just a simple border
options.effect: Avoids adding another cluttering layer of color; keeps neutral balance.
options.when: When cards only need to be separated.

decisions.recommendation: Lighten the brand color and use black text, or drop the background and use a simple border; the source says adding another colored layer is a lot of clutter.
decisions.evidence: swap the cards for our brand color; sometimes a simple border is the best solution

decisions.question: How much of the screen should accent color cover?

options.name: Many competing accents
options.effect: At least five accents on the cards all compete for attention, and most fail WCAG contrast.
options.when: Not recommended.

options.name: Brand color on large secondary surfaces
options.effect: Somewhat hits 60-30-10, but the bright brand color dominates the page for an element that isn't important.
options.when: Not for low-importance elements.

options.name: 60-30-10 split
options.effect: 60% dominant neutral, 30% secondary, 10% accent; it also works with bold colors, as Lemon Squeezy shows.
options.when: As a rough check on the balance of a screen.

decisions.recommendation: Use less color: one accent kept off unimportant elements, with 60-30-10 as a loose guide rather than a strict rule.
decisions.evidence: Less is almost always more with color; all competing for attention

decisions.question: Should icons be colored?

options.name: Colored icons
options.effect: Adds more competing color to the screen.
options.when: Not recommended by default.

options.name: Uncolored icons, color only for status
options.effect: Icons read as recognizable symbols, and color signals status such as the active tab.
options.when: Default.

decisions.recommendation: Mostly no color; reserve color for status like the active tab.

decisions.question: What should backgrounds and foregrounds look like?

options.name: Bright color or gradient background
options.effect: The background stops staying in the background (the sandy yellow gradient).
options.when: Almost never; the source allows notable exceptions.

options.name: Neutral gray background, white or very light foreground
options.effect: Backgrounds recede and content stands out, like white space does for hierarchy.
options.when: General starting point in light mode.

options.name: Reversed background and foreground
options.effect: Small features stand out with better accessibility.
options.when: Light mode, for smaller UI features such as Dribbble's search bar.

options.name: Neutral gray with a hint of the brand hue
options.effect: Adds a splash of color without overpowering the visuals (Headspace's orange tint on cards).
options.when: When you want a little more brand color in the neutrals.

decisions.recommendation: Start with a neutral gray background and a very light or white foreground; tinting the neutral toward the brand hue is an option.
decisions.evidence: start with a neutral gray background and a very light or white foreground

decisions.question: Should neutral grays be pure or tinted toward the brand color?

options.name: Pure neutral gray
options.effect: Backgrounds stay fully neutral.
options.when: The plain starting point.

options.name: Neutral gray with a hint of the brand hue
options.effect: Brings a little brand color into backgrounds without overpowering visuals.
options.when: To integrate more color, as Headspace does with its orange.

decisions.evidence: taking our neutral gray and adding a hint of purple to it

decisions.question: The brand guidelines give too few colors. How do you get more colors for things like a storage bar?

options.name: Change the brand color's opacity
options.effect: Works but feels a little bland.
options.when: When a quiet variation is enough.

options.name: Analogous: rotate the brand hue slightly
options.effect: Adds related colors (a blue and a pinkish color from purple) that sit well together.
options.when: To add variety that stays close to the brand.

options.name: Complementary: cross the color wheel
options.effect: Adds a contrasting color (bright yellow opposite purple) that still works with the brand.
options.when: When you need a color that pops against the brand, or when the brand color fails contrast.

decisions.recommendation: Rotate the hue or pick a complementary color rather than only changing opacity; brands like Mailchimp and Airbnb do this.
decisions.evidence: rotate our purple slightly on the color wheel

decisions.question: The brand color fails WCAG contrast with white text. What do you do?

options.name: Darken the brand color
options.effect: The darker version passes with white text.
options.when: When the brand hue must stay.

options.name: Use a complementary color
options.effect: A complementary blue also passes with white text.
options.when: When a secondary color can carry that job.

decisions.recommendation: Either works; don't be afraid to adapt brand colors to accommodate good design.
decisions.evidence: fails WCAG checks with white text

decisions.question: What color should less important text, labels and borders be?

options.name: Pure black (or pure white in dark mode)
options.effect: Everything has the same weight, so hierarchy is weaker.
options.when: Not bad in itself; best kept for the most important items.

options.name: Dark or light gray (or a very dark brand hue)
options.effect: Secondary information recedes and hierarchy becomes clear.
options.when: File size and type, labels, borders; most text in the redesign is light gray or dark purple.

decisions.recommendation: Use more gray and less black and white; the source says this separates mediocre from professional designers.
decisions.evidence: Using pure white and pure black is not bad

decisions.question: How should dark mode be made from light mode?

options.name: Invert the light-mode colors
options.effect: Not awful, but certainly not ideal: borders and cards lack separation and all text turns light purple.
options.when: Not recommended.

options.name: Build the palette with dark-mode goals in mind
options.effect: Brighter borders and cards, light gray text, pure white only on the most important text, a slightly desaturated logo.
options.when: Recommended.

decisions.recommendation: Build the palette for dark mode on purpose rather than inverting.
decisions.evidence: you shouldn't just inverse your colors from light to dark

decisions.question: Should a delete button use the brand color or red?

options.name: Brand color background
options.effect: More on brand, but it draws attention to the button and doesn't show it is destructive.
options.when: Not for destructive actions.

options.name: Red background
options.effect: Clearly signals a destructive action.
options.when: Delete and other destructive actions.

decisions.recommendation: Use red; a brand-colored destructive action wouldn't fly from a usability point of view.
decisions.evidence: we can either have the delete button have a purple background or a red background

decisions.question: What color should notification indicators be?

options.name: Red
options.effect: The common convention for notifications.
options.when: Default choice.

options.name: Brand color
options.effect: Stays on brand.
options.when: Acceptable, since notifications are much more flexible than destructive actions.

decisions.recommendation: Either; the source says notifications could be swapped to the brand color.
decisions.evidence: Red is also often used for notifications

decisions.question: Which interactive states should be designed, and does it differ on mobile?

options.name: Hover, press and disabled
options.effect: Hover is slightly lighter or brighter, press slightly darker, disabled desaturated.
options.when: Pointer devices where hover exists.

options.name: Press only (plus disabled)
options.effect: A slightly darker gray on press makes it feel like pressing into something.
options.when: Mobile, which has no hover effects.

decisions.recommendation: Use lighter for hover, darker for press, desaturated for disabled; on mobile rely on press effects.
decisions.evidence: because we don't have hover effects on mobile, we usually just resort to click effects

process.detail: Replace multiple accent colors with the brand color, lighten it for unimportant elements with black text, strip color from icons except for status, and remove colors used only for the sake of color.

Make backgrounds a neutral gray with white or very light foregrounds (darker background, lighter foreground in dark mode), optionally tint the gray toward the brand hue, and use a simple border instead of another colored layer where possible.
Where brand guidelines give too few colors, rotate the brand hue slightly for analogous colors or cross the wheel for a complementary one; darken or swap brand colors that fail WCAG with white text.
Move secondary text, labels and borders from black to dark or light grays; keep pure black or white for the most important items.

Starting from the light palette, brighten borders and main surfaces, use light grays for text, brighten only the most important text to pure white, lower gray brightness more aggressively, and desaturate the logo a touch.
Use red for destructive actions such as delete and keep red and green in the palette; notifications can use red or the brand color.
Hover: slightly lighter or brighter. Press: slightly darker. Disabled: desaturated (light gray with white text). On mobile, add press states, since there is no hover.

caveats: Sponsor segment for Final Round AI (job search), repeated at the end; not design advice.
Self-promotion: a resources page on kolejain.com and the Figma files in the description.
Auto-caption errors: '603010' is the 60-30-10 rule and the 'BY' before it is a mis-hearing; 'complimentary' means complementary; 'dribble' is Dribbble.
The seven mistakes are not numbered in the transcript; the list in key_ideas is an inferred grouping.
The source treats 60-30-10 loosely (the redesign only 'somewhat' hits it); OpenDesigner's Q-color-05 already treats 60-30-10 as a soft check [inferred]
Several statements are opinion, such as using more gray being what separates mediocre from professional designers.
Brand examples (Lemon Squeezy, Headspace, Dribbble, Mailchimp, Airbnb) reflect their designs around the September 2025 publish date and may have changed.
Color values (hex codes, exact contrast ratios, tint amounts) are shown on screen but not stated in the transcript, so none are recorded here.
The hint of purple in the neutral gray and the Headspace tint are introduced right after the dark-mode point, so it is unclear whether the source means dark mode only or both modes.

Strength 'must' is used only where the transcript is firm (WCAG failures 'we can't reasonably use', an on-brand delete button 'wouldn't fly'); other points are hedged ('almost always', 'not bad', 'notable exceptions') and kept as should or consider.
